top5.diagnosis: Metastatic Cutaneous Melanoma to Oral Cavity
top5.rationale: Must rule out primary skin melanoma metastasizing to oral mucosa given the pigmentation and nodal involvement; requires full-body dermatologic exam.
Can present as pigmented vascular lesions on gingiva/palate; consider if patient has undiagnosed HIV or immunosuppression despite normal initial labs.
Common benign vascular lesion that can appear dark due to thrombosis/hemosiderin, but fixed lymph node makes this less likely than malignancy.

top5.diagnosis: Amalgam Tattoo with Concurrent Squamous Cell Carcinoma
top5.rationale: Incidental pigmentation from dental history masking an underlying non-pigmented carcinoma causing the mass effect and nodal spread.

The classic presentation of a painless, enlarging pigmented gingival lesion with tooth displacement and regional lymphadenopathy is the hallmark of this malignancy; alternative diagnoses rarely present with this specific combination of pigment and aggressive local behavior.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic Cutaneous Melanoma to Oral Cavity
top5.rationale: While primary oral melanoma is rare, metastasis from an occult or previously excised cutaneous site can mimic a primary lesion; however, the lack of reported skin history makes this less likely than primary disease but remains a critical differential for any pigmented mass.

This vascular tumor can present as a pigmented (purple/black) gingival mass with high vascularity on ultrasound, matching the imaging findings; however, it is typically associated with immunosuppression (HIV/transplant), which is absent in this patient's history.

SCC is the most common oral malignancy and can cause tooth displacement and necrotic nodes; while usually non-pigmented, rare variants or secondary hemorrhage/necrosis can appear dark, though true black pigmentation strongly favors melanocytic origin.

These tumors can arise in the head/neck region, be firm, and cause bone/tooth displacement; they are occasionally pigmented due to melanin production by Schwann cells, but this is exceptionally rare compared to mucosal melanoma.
Pigmented gingival lesion with tooth displacement and necrotic cervical lymphadenopathy is the classic presentation; normal labs exclude systemic metabolic causes.
The 'highly vascular mass' on ultrasound and pigmented appearance fit KS, though lack of HIV history or other lesions makes it less likely than melanoma.
RCC is a known cause of highly vascular, hypervascular metastases to the head/neck that can mimic primary tumors; requires renal imaging to rule out.
These tumors are characteristically highly vascular with low-velocity waveforms and can present as firm, painless masses in the oral cavity.
A rare malignant vascular tumor that presents as a pigmented, rapidly growing, highly vascular mass with early nodal spread.
Classic presentation in a young patient with severe, longstanding T1DM and microvascular complications; MRI showing muscle edema/atrophy without abscess or DVT is pathognomonic.

High-risk demographic (Indigenous Australian, remote community) combined with immunocompromise (poorly controlled DM, smoking) and systemic inflammation makes bacterial muscle infection a critical differential to exclude despite lack of frank pus on initial imaging.
Severe nutritional deficiency (Vit C 12 µmol/L) in a cachectic smoker can cause subperiosteal/intramuscular hemorrhage and pain mimicking inflammatory myopathy or infarction.

Recurrent UTIs and nephropathy suggest potential hematogenous seeding or contiguous spread from undiagnosed bone pathology, though normal CK and specific muscle-only MRI findings make this less likely than primary muscle disease.

Must be considered in any persistent deep soft tissue mass/swelling in a young adult, but the diffuse nature, bilateral microvascular context, and rapid inflammatory markers favor metabolic/infectious etiologies over neoplasm.

Classic triad of long-standing poorly controlled T1DM with microvascular complications, acute painful thigh swelling without trauma/infection signs, and MRI showing muscle edema/infarction; histology would show coagulative necrosis and vascular hyalinization.

High inflammatory markers (CRP 185, ESR 120) and leukocytosis in an immunocompromised host (poorly controlled DM, malnutrition) mimic DMI; requires exclusion via culture/biopsy as it is a bacterial infection (often S. aureus) of skeletal muscle.

top5.diagnosis: Scurvy (Vitamin C Deficiency) with Hemorrhagic Myopathy
top5.rationale: Severe vitamin C deficiency (12 µmol/L) causes defective collagen synthesis leading to vessel fragility, intramuscular hemorrhage, pain, and swelling that can radiologically mimic infarction or abscess in cachectic patients.

top5.diagnosis: Soft Tissue Sarcoma (e.g., Undifferentiated Pleomorphic Sarcoma)
top5.rationale: Must be ruled out given the large mass-like effect on CT/MRI; however, lack of discrete mass, diffuse nature, and strong association with diabetic microangiopathy make this less likely than metabolic/ischemic etiologies.

End-stage renal disease context (nephrotic syndrome, CKD) and severe inflammation could drive small-vessel calcification and ischemic necrosis, though typically presents with skin lesions which are absent here.
Classic presentation of painful thigh swelling in poorly controlled T1DM with microvascular complications; MRI showing muscle edema without abscess and normal CK is pathognomonic.
Must be ruled out due to leukocytosis, high CRP/ESR, and diabetes as a risk factor, though lack of fluid collection on CT/MRI makes this less likely than infarction.

top5.diagnosis: Scurvy (Vitamin C Deficiency) with Musculoskeletal Manifestations
top5.rationale: Severe vitamin C deficiency (12 µmol/L) in a cachectic patient can cause subperiosteal hemorrhage and myalgia mimicking inflammatory or ischemic processes.
High inflammatory markers and remote community background raise suspicion for hematogenous spread, though imaging localizes pathology primarily to muscle rather than bone marrow.
A mass-like lesion in the thigh requires exclusion, but diffuse low attenuation without a discrete solid mass on CT and the clinical context of severe vascular disease favor benign etiology.
The leading hypothesis, but challenged by the extreme cachexia and nutritional deficits which may be primary drivers rather than secondary effects.

top5.diagnosis: Scurvy (Vitamin C Deficiency) with Secondary Myopathy
top5.rationale: Explains the profound weight loss, anemia, thrombocytosis, elevated inflammatory markers, and muscle pain/swelling in a malnourished patient better than DMI alone.
High leukocytosis, CRP, and ESR in an immunocompromised host suggest infection; MRI findings of edema can mimic infarction, and abscess formation may be early or diffuse.
Hypoalbuminemia <15 g/L and BMI 12.9 indicate starvation physiology causing muscle wasting, edema, and immune dysregulation that mimics organic disease.
Unexplained by benign diagnoses: persistent mass effect, severe systemic inflammation, and cachexia in a young adult warrant exclusion despite 'ill-defined' imaging.
The reproducible cough upon palpation is a pathognomonic sign of vagal nerve involvement, and the mass location within the carotid sheath with minimal splaying fits this neurogenic tumor profile.
A primary differential for any mass in the carotid sheath causing vagal symptoms; while less likely to cause the specific 'cough reflex' than paragangliomas, it remains a top structural candidate.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic Squamous Cell Carcinoma (Level II Node)
top5.rationale: In a 70-year-old smoker or non-smoker, a necrotic Level II node is statistically common, though the specific mechanical cough trigger makes a benign neurogenic origin more probable.
Classic carotid sheath tumor, but typically causes significant splaying of the internal and external carotid arteries ('lyre sign'), which was explicitly noted as minimal here.
Another peripheral nerve sheath tumor that can occupy the carotid space and compress adjacent structures, though usually associated with NF1 which was denied.

The pathognomonic 'cough reflex' upon palpation indicates direct vagal nerve involvement, while the carotid sheath location and intense enhancement fit a neuroendocrine tumor arising from paraganglia.

A benign nerve sheath tumor in the carotid sheath can mechanically irritate the vagus nerve causing cough; however, it typically displaces rather than splays vessels and lacks the hypervascular 'salt-and-pepper' MRI signature of paragangliomas.

While classically presenting with splaying of the internal and external carotid arteries (Lyre sign), atypical presentations or smaller tumors may primarily manifest with cranial nerve symptoms like cough before significant vascular distortion is evident.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic Squamous Cell Carcinoma to Cervical Lymph Node
top5.rationale: A necrotic, enhancing mass in level II is highly suspicious for metastasis from an occult head/neck primary; however, the specific reproducibility of cough on palpation strongly favors a neural origin over simple nodal compression.

Similar to schwannoma, this peripheral nerve sheath tumor can cause vagal irritation, but it is less likely given the lack of Neurofibromatosis history and the distinct imaging characteristics described.
The reproducible cough upon palpation is a pathognomonic mechanical sign of vagal nerve involvement, and the carotid sheath location with intense enhancement fits this neuroendocrine tumor profile.
While less likely to cause the specific 'cough reflex' than paragangliomas, schwannomas are common carotid sheath masses that can compress or irritate the vagus nerve, causing hoarseness and cough.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic Squamous Cell Carcinoma (Level II Lymph Node)
top5.rationale: A necrotic, irregular mass in an elderly patient with a dry cough raises concern for malignancy, though the lack of a primary head/neck lesion and the specific neural trigger make this less likely than benign neurogenic tumors.

Typically causes splaying of the internal and external carotid arteries; however, the minimal splaying and lateral position relative to the vessels make a vagal origin more probable than a carotid body origin.
Similar to schwannoma but often associated with NF1; given the unremarkable family history and lack of other stigmata, this is a lower probability differential for a solitary carotid sheath mass.
The hallmark 'cough reflex' triggered by palpation of a carotid sheath mass is pathognomonic for vagal nerve involvement, distinguishing it from carotid body tumors.
A benign neural sheath tumor in the same anatomical location can compress or irritate the vagus nerve, eliciting the cough reflex, though less commonly than paragangliomas.

While classically associated with splaying of the carotid bifurcation and pulsatility, atypical presentations or smaller lesions may still cause local nerve irritation; however, the lack of splaying makes this less likely.
Similar to schwannoma, this peripheral nerve sheath tumor could present as a mobile neck mass causing vagal symptoms, though usually associated with NF1 which was denied.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic Squamous Cell Carcinoma Lymph Node
top5.rationale: In a 70-year-old smoker (implied risk) or non-smoker, a necrotic level II node is a top differential for malignancy, but the specific reproducible cough reflex strongly favors a primary neural origin over simple nodal compression.
Explains the cough triggered by palpation (vagal irritation) and hoarseness better than paraganglioma, which typically spares nerve function until late; necrosis is possible in ancient schwannomas.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic Squamous Cell Carcinoma to Level II Node
top5.rationale: Most common cause of a necrotic lateral neck mass in this age group; can invade or compress the vagus nerve causing cough/hoarseness, though primary source must be sought.
Classic location and vascularity, but minimal arterial splaying and normal catecholamines make it less likely than neural tumors for this specific presentation of prominent vagal symptoms.
Similar symptom profile to schwannoma due to vagal involvement, but less likely given lack of NF1 history and solitary nature; still a key differential for intravagal masses.
Rare but aggressive; fits the rapid onset (4 weeks), irregular/necrotic imaging features, and neurological deficits, though usually associated with NF1 or prior radiation.
Unifies the markedly elevated serum IgG4, positive salivary gland biopsy (sialadenitis), and cholestatic liver enzymes with the hemodynamic and imaging findings of constrictive pericarditis.

A classic mimic that must be ruled out in constrictive physiology; however, negative QuantiFERON and lack of systemic inflammatory markers make this less likely than IgG4-RD given the specific serologic evidence.
Explains the cardiac mechanics but fails to account for the extra-cardiac manifestations (sialadenitis, hepatic enzyme elevation) and the highly specific IgG4 serology/biopsy results.

Can cause constrictive physiology and multi-organ disease (including salivary glands), but typically presents with different histopathology (non-caseating granulomas vs. IgG4 plasma cells) and normal IgG4 levels.

top5.diagnosis: Primary Sjögren's syndrome with secondary amyloidosis or autoimmune pericarditis
top5.rationale: Accounts for sialadenitis and potential cardiac issues, but does not explain the massive IgG4 elevation, the specific biopsy ratio, or the calcific constrictive pattern as well as IgG4-RD.

top5.diagnosis: IgG4-related disease with constrictive pericarditis and sialadenitis
top5.rationale: The triad of markedly elevated serum IgG4, histologic confirmation in salivary gland, and imaging/hemodynamic evidence of constrictive physiology (pericardial calcification, equalization of pressures) defines this systemic fibro-inflammatory process.

While hemodynamics fit constriction perfectly, the absence of a unifying systemic etiology like IgG4-RD would make this a diagnosis of exclusion, which is less likely given the specific serologic and histologic findings present.
A classic cause of constrictive pericarditis with calcification; however, it is effectively ruled out by the negative QuantiFERON-TB Gold test and lack of typical infectious inflammatory markers.
Can mimic IgG4-RD or idiopathic constriction with calcification and fibrosis, but there is no history of thoracic radiation provided to support this mechanism.

Can cause restrictive/constrictive physiology and glandular swelling, but typically presents with non-caseating granulomas rather than IgG4-rich lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, and ANCA/ACE levels are not mentioned as supportive.

top5.diagnosis: IgG4-related disease (manifesting as constrictive pericarditis and sialadenitis)
top5.rationale: Serum IgG4 >10x normal, histopathologic confirmation in salivary gland, and imaging/hemodynamic evidence of constrictive physiology (pericardial calcification, equalized pressures, septal bounce) create a unifying diagnosis.

Hemodynamics (dip-and-plateau, systolic area index >1.6) and CT findings are classic for constriction, but this is less likely than IgG4-RD given the specific serologic and biopsy evidence pointing to an etiology.

A major differential for constrictive pericarditis with calcification; however, the negative QuantiFERON-TB Gold and lack of systemic inflammatory markers make this significantly less likely than IgG4-RD.

top5.diagnosis: Sjögren's syndrome with secondary cardiac involvement
top5.rationale: Sialadenitis might suggest Sjögren's, but the absence of anti-Ro/La antibodies (implied by negative autoimmune panel context), high IgG4 levels, and specific constrictive hemodynamics favor IgG4-RD over primary Sjögren's.

top5.diagnosis: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) exacerbation due to restrictive cardiomyopathy
top5.rationale: The patient has known HFpEF, but the echocardiographic finding of significant respiratory variation in E-velocity and pericardial calcification points to pericardial constraint rather than intrinsic myocardial restriction alone.

Serum IgG4 >135 mg/dL, salivary gland biopsy showing >10 IgG4+ cells/HPF and high IgG4/IgG ratio, combined with pericardial calcification/constriction and cholestatic liver enzymes typical of IgG4-related sclerosing disease.

top5.diagnosis: Constrictive pericarditis secondary to IgG4-related pericardial disease
top5.rationale: Hemodynamic findings (equalized filling pressures, dip-and-plateau, septal bounce) and CT evidence of pericardial calcification in an elderly patient without prior surgery or radiation strongly suggest chronic inflammatory constriction driven by the underlying systemic IgG4 process.

The development of sialadenitis is a classic head-and-neck manifestation of IgG4-RD, serving as a critical diagnostic clue linking the cardiac and hepatic findings to a single systemic etiology rather than isolated organ failure.

Elevated GGT and alkaline phosphatase with mild bilirubin elevation indicate biliary obstruction or infiltration, consistent with IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis, which often co-occurs with other organ manifestations in this demographic.

Must be considered in any case of constrictive pericarditis with calcification; however, it is ranked lower due to negative QuantiFERON-TB Gold and the overwhelming serologic/biopsy evidence for IgG4-RD, though latent TB reactivation remains a theoretical differential in immunocompromised hosts.

The brother's paradoxical cortisol increase with dexamethasone is pathognomonic for PBMAH, and the sister's presentation represents the same genetic entity manifesting with asymmetric nodularity rather than diffuse enlargement.

The occurrence in two siblings with identical biochemical profiles (ACTH-independent Cushing's) strongly suggests a hereditary syndrome, likely involving germline mutations in genes such as PRKACA or ARMC5.

This is the most common cause of ACTH-independent Cushing's syndrome and fits the sister's unilateral nodule, but it fails to explain the brother's bilateral disease and paradoxical dexamethasone response.
Must be considered in any adrenal mass with rapid-onset severe hypercortisolism, though the small size of the sister's nodule and the chronic course in the brother make this highly unlikely.
Included as a differential for adrenal masses and hypertension, but the clinical phenotype is dominated by glucocorticoid excess rather than catecholamine excess, making this incorrect.
Paradoxical cortisol rise on Liddle's test and bilateral adrenal nodularity in siblings strongly indicate PPNAD, often associated with Carney complex.
PPNAD is the hallmark endocrine manifestation of this autosomal dominant syndrome caused by PRKAR1A mutations, explaining the familial clustering.
Bilateral adrenal enlargement/nodules with suppressed ACTH fits AIMAH, though the paradoxical dexamethasone response favors PPNAD over classic AIMAH.
Unlikely due to suppressed ACTH (<5 pg/mL) and lack of central suppression, but must be ruled out if assay interference or ectopic production exists.
Excluded by low ACTH levels; however, rare cases of ectopic CRH secretion can mimic primary adrenal disease, though less likely given the specific adrenal morphology.

The combination of markedly elevated serum IgG4, diagnostic salivary gland biopsy, and imaging/hemodynamic evidence of constrictive physiology (pericardial calcification, equalization of pressures, septal bounce) provides a unified explanation for both the cardiac decompensation and the sialadenitis.

Despite negative QuantiFERON, TB remains a top differential for constrictive pericarditis in elderly patients; however, it fails to explain the specific IgG4 serology and histopathology, making it less likely than IgG4-RD.

A diagnosis of exclusion that fits the hemodynamic and imaging findings but ignores the striking extra-cardiac manifestations (sialadenitis) and abnormal immunologic markers which point toward a systemic etiology.

top5.diagnosis: Sjögren's syndrome with secondary cardiac involvement
top5.rationale: Explains the sialadenitis and potential autoimmune background, but does not account for the high IgG4 levels, the specific histological ratio, or the classic constrictive pericarditis physiology as well as IgG4-RD does.

Can present with heart failure and biatrial enlargement in an elderly diabetic patient, but the presence of pericardial calcifications, dip-and-plateau pattern, and respiratory variation strongly favors true constriction over restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Explains ACTH-independent Cushing's in both siblings with paradoxical dexamethasone response and bilateral adrenal abnormalities, unlike unilateral adenoma.
Rare genetic cause of hypercortisolism that can present with Cushingoid features due to compensatory high cortisol levels despite receptor resistance, fitting the familial pattern.

top5.diagnosis: Autonomous Cortisol-Secreting Adrenal Adenoma (Sister) with Incidental Findings (Brother)
top5.rationale: Challenges the leading hypothesis by suggesting the sister has a true adenoma while the brother's findings may be misinterpreted or represent a different, non-Cushing pathology like simple obesity/striae.

Can cause autonomous endocrine hyperfunction including Cushing syndrome via GNAS mutations, potentially presenting with bilateral adrenal involvement and bone disease, though skin pigmentation is absent here.
Considers exogenous glucocorticoid use as an alternative explanation for suppressed ACTH and failed suppression tests, particularly if family members share access to medications.

top5.diagnosis: Primary Bilateral Macronodular Adrenal Hyperplasia (PBMAH) with autonomous cortisol secretion
top5.rationale: ACTH-independent Cushing's syndrome in siblings with bilateral adrenal enlargement/nodules and paradoxical Liddle's test response strongly suggests PBMAH rather than unilateral adenoma.

top5.diagnosis: Familial Glucocorticoid-Induced Mineralocorticoid Excess (GIME) or similar familial adrenal hyperplasia variant
top5.rationale: The familial clustering of ACTH-independent hypercortisolism with specific imaging patterns (diffuse vs nodular) points to a genetic etiology like GIME or MEN1-associated adrenal disease, though GIME typically presents earlier.

While less likely given the chronicity and bilateral involvement, ACC must be ruled out in any young patient with severe osteoporosis and rapid weight gain; however, the bilateral nature makes this highly improbable unless metastatic.

top5.diagnosis: Ectopic ACTH Syndrome with adrenal hyperplasia
top5.rationale: Unlikely due to suppressed ACTH (<5 pg/mL), but included as a differential for severe Cushing's if assay interference or intermittent secretion is suspected, which would explain the discordant imaging findings.

top5.diagnosis: Incidental Adrenal Adenoma masking underlying Primary Aldosteronism or other pathology
top5.rationale: The 'adenoma' on CT may be a red herring; the true driver could be diffuse hyperplasia not fully characterized by standard CT, requiring functional imaging (NP-59 or PET) to distinguish benign from malignant or hyperplastic tissue.

top5.diagnosis: Disseminated Histoplasmosis with Primary Adrenal Involvement
top5.rationale: The biopsy confirms Histoplasma spores in necrotic adrenal tissue, explaining the bilateral masses, pancytopenia (bone marrow infiltration), and subsequent acute adrenal crisis.

top5.diagnosis: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency secondary to Infectious Destruction
top5.rationale: The clinical presentation of hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and low cortisol is a direct physiological consequence of the fungal destruction of the adrenal glands.

A critical differential in Sri Lanka presenting with identical features (bilateral adrenal masses, fever, weight loss); ruled out by negative Mantoux/biopsy stains but clinically indistinguishable until histology.
Bilateral homogeneous adrenal masses with systemic B-symptoms and lymphadenopathy are classic for primary adrenal lymphoma, though the specific fungal staining excludes this.
Common cause of bilateral adrenal masses and constitutional symptoms; however, the lack of a known primary tumor and the presence of infectious organisms on biopsy make this unlikely.
The brother's paradoxical cortisol increase with dexamethasone and bilateral adrenal nodularity are pathognomonic for PBMAH, which can present in siblings due to shared genetic susceptibility.
Suppressed ACTH (<5 pg/mL) in both patients confirms the etiology is adrenal rather than pituitary or ectopic, ruling out Cushing Disease despite the classic phenotype.

The combination of hypercortisolism, hypertension, and hypokalemia-like features (though electrolytes normal here) with familial clustering suggests a rare autosomal dominant defect in the glucocorticoid receptor leading to compensatory adrenal hyperplasia.

Although less likely given the chronicity and bilateral nature, the rapid weight gain, severe osteoporosis, and large adrenal changes in a young patient require exclusion of malignancy as a differential for primary adrenal Cushing's.

top5.diagnosis: Incidental Adrenal Adenoma with Subclinical Cushing's
top5.rationale: The sister's unilateral nodule may be an incidental finding masking a more diffuse bilateral process like PBMAH, a common diagnostic pitfall when imaging focuses on the most prominent lesion.
Epidemiologically plausible in Sri Lanka; adrenal tropism explains the bilateral masses and subsequent primary adrenal insufficiency crisis.

top5.diagnosis: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison's Disease) secondary to Fungal Infection
top5.rationale: The clinical presentation of hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and low cortisol is a direct physiological consequence of the identified fungal destruction of adrenal tissue.
Must be considered in any patient with bilateral adrenal masses and B-symptoms (fever, weight loss), though less likely given the specific fungal histology.
High epidemiological prevalence in Sri Lanka and classic cause of bilateral adrenal enlargement, but ruled out by negative Mantoux, cultures, and lack of caseating granulomas on biopsy.
Common cause of bilateral adrenal masses, but unlikely due to absence of a known primary tumor, normal chest imaging, and benign inflammatory/fungal nature of the biopsy.

Biopsy-proven fungal spores in adrenal tissue explain the primary pathology: bilateral adrenal destruction causing acute adrenal crisis (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypotension) and systemic symptoms (fever, pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly).

Bilateral homogeneous adrenal masses with B-symptoms and para-aortic lymphadenopathy are classic for DLBCL; however, the specific GMS-positive fungal morphology on biopsy makes this a mimic rather than the true cause.

Bilateral adrenal masses often represent metastases (e.g., lung, melanoma), but the absence of a primary tumor on imaging and the presence of infectious organisms on histology exclude this as the primary driver.

A leading differential for bilateral adrenal enlargement with necrosis and constitutional symptoms in endemic regions; ruled out by negative Mantoux, bone marrow studies, and the distinct yeast-like morphology of Histoplasma vs. acid-fast bacilli.

Presents with adrenal insufficiency and autoimmune markers, but does not account for the large bilateral adrenal masses, significant lymphadenopathy, or the infectious etiology confirmed by silver stain.
Temporal correlation with drug infusion and classic signs of distributive shock, bronchospasm, and angioedema despite absence of cutaneous urticaria.
NSAIDs are known to trigger direct mast cell activation via COX-1 inhibition, explaining the reaction without prior sensitization or IgE involvement.
The presence of frequent premature supraventricular and ventricular contractions alongside hypotension suggests mast-cell mediator-induced coronary vasospasm or plaque erosion.
Although rare in short-term use, propofol can cause cardiovascular collapse; however, the specific timing linked to diclofenac makes this less likely than anaphylaxis.
IVF patients are hypercoagulable, and PE causes hypotension and hypoxia, but it does not explain the rapid onset of angioedema, secretions, and bronchospasm immediately following drug administration.

The biopsy definitively identifies Histoplasma spores; this single diagnosis explains the pancytopenia (bone marrow infiltration), hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, bilateral adrenal masses, and subsequent primary adrenal insufficiency without requiring multiple concurrent pathologies.

Bilateral homogeneous adrenal masses with systemic B-symptoms and para-aortic lymphadenopathy are classic for lymphoma, but this is excluded by the specific fungal staining on biopsy, making it a strong alternative only if the stain were misinterpreted.

A leading differential in Sri Lanka causing bilateral adrenal destruction and constitutional symptoms, but ruled out by negative Mantoux, bone marrow TB studies, and the presence of fungal rather than acid-fast bacilli on biopsy.

Bilateral adrenal masses often suggest metastasis, but the lack of a known primary tumor, normal chest imaging, and the inflammatory/necrotic nature of the biopsy with fungal elements make this highly unlikely compared to infection.

Explains adrenal failure and diabetes, but fails to account for the large bilateral adrenal masses, pancytopenia, fever, or the histological evidence of fungal infection, representing an incomplete fit.

top5.diagnosis: Disseminated Histoplasmosis with Primary Adrenal Involvement
top5.rationale: The definitive biopsy showing GMS-positive fungal spores morphologically consistent with Histoplasma in the context of bilateral adrenal masses and necrosis confirms this as the primary pathology.

top5.diagnosis: Acute Adrenal Crisis secondary to Histoplasmosis
top5.rationale: The clinical triad of refractory hypotension, severe hyponatremia (114 mmol/L), hyperkalemia, and undetectable cortisol (<1 µg/L) indicates life-threatening adrenal insufficiency caused by the destruction of adrenal tissue.

top5.diagnosis: Pancytopenia due to Bone Marrow Infiltration or Hypersplenism
top5.rationale: Initial pancytopenia with hepatosplenomegaly suggests marrow infiltration by disseminated fungi or sequestration, which paradoxically improved after fluid resuscitation and likely partial treatment response.

The presentation of constitutional symptoms, night sweats, weight loss, and para-aortic lymphadenopathy in a Sri Lankan patient strongly mimics TB or lymphoma, explaining the initial negative Mantoux and bone marrow workup for those conditions.

While present in the history, the diet-controlled status and normal HbA1c suggest it is not driving the acute crisis; however, diabetes may have predisposed the patient to more severe dissemination of the fungal infection.
Temporal correlation with drug infusion, classic hemodynamic collapse, bronchospasm, and angioedema despite absence of cutaneous signs.
NSAIDs can trigger direct mast cell degranulation or COX-1 inhibition pathways without prior sensitization, fitting the immediate onset.

top5.diagnosis: Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS) with acute decompensation
top5.rationale: High follicle count (>30) is a major risk factor; fluid shifts and capillary leak could exacerbate hypotension and respiratory compromise.
IVF increases thrombotic risk; sudden hypoxia, tachycardia, and hypotension fit PE, though bronchospasm/angioedema makes this less likely than allergy.
Sedation for procedure carries aspiration risk; secretions and hypoxia are present, but rapid resolution with adrenaline argues against primary lung injury.
Temporal causality is strongest; absence of cutaneous signs does not exclude anaphylaxis, especially with severe respiratory/cardiovascular collapse and angioedema.
A common culprit in anesthesia that may have had a delayed or synergistic presentation triggered by the subsequent drug infusion.
Often overlooked in non-surgical settings; exposure via gloves or tubing during IV access/aspiration could cause identical symptoms without skin rash initially.
IVF increases thrombotic risk; explains hypotension, tachycardia, and low EtCO2, but fails to explain secretions, rhonchi, and facial edema.
Possible given airway manipulation, but typically presents with hypoxia and infiltrates rather than immediate distributive shock and angioedema.
Temporal association with NSAID infusion causing distributive shock, bronchospasm, and angioedema without cutaneous signs (common in severe cases), supported by tryptase testing.
Delayed presentation is atypical but possible; propofol contains egg lecithin/soybean oil which can trigger IgE-mediated reactions, though usually immediate upon induction.
Rare benzodiazepine hypersensitivity reaction that could present with similar hemodynamic collapse and airway compromise, often overlooked due to low incidence.
Exposure via gloves or equipment during IVF procedure; presents identically to drug anaphylaxis and is a critical differential in healthcare-associated anaphylaxis.
Mast cell mediator release causing coronary vasospasm leading to the observed arrhythmias (PVCs/SVT) and hypotension, potentially secondary to any of the above triggers.
Unifies hypophosphatemic rickets features (bowing, fractures, hearing loss, dental abscesses) with enthesopathy mimicking AS; negative HLA-B27 and NSAID failure support non-inflammatory etiology.
Acquired hypophosphatemia causing similar skeletal/enthesopathic changes, though less likely given the childhood onset of hearing loss and dental issues.
Initial clinical diagnosis based on imaging, but contradicted by negative HLA-B27, lack of response to biologics/NSAIDs, and presence of metabolic bone disease markers.
Clinically indistinguishable from XLH in adult presentation; requires genetic testing to differentiate, but fits all phenotypic features including enthesopathy.
Explains spinal ligament calcification and enthesophytes, but fails to account for hypophosphatemia, femoral bowing, or early-onset hearing/dental pathology.
Temporal correlation with IV diclofenac infusion, classic hemodynamic collapse, bronchospasm, and angioedema despite absence of cutaneous signs.

top5.diagnosis: Non-IgE mediated mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS)
top5.rationale: Severe reaction to NSAID in a patient with no prior allergy history suggests direct mast cell degranulation rather than IgE-mediated sensitization.

top5.diagnosis: Propofol-related infusion syndrome (PRIS) or severe propofol hypersensitivity
top5.rationale: Although rare after single bolus, propofol is a known allergen; however, the immediate trigger was diclofenac, making this a less likely primary cause but a confounding factor in polypharmacy anesthesia.

top5.diagnosis: Pulmonary embolism secondary to IVF hypercoagulability
top5.rationale: IVF patients are at high risk for thrombosis; PE can mimic anaphylaxis with hypotension and hypoxia, though the rapid resolution with adrenaline and lack of D-dimer elevation mentioned makes it less likely.
Ultrasound-guided procedure under sedation carries aspiration risk; could explain secretions and hypoxia, but does not account for the profound vasodilatory shock and angioedema seen here.

Classic triad of childhood-onset hearing loss, dental abscesses/fractures due to defective dentin mineralization, and adult-onset osteomalacia with insufficiency fractures; hypophosphatemia with inappropriate renal phosphate wasting and elevated PTH confirms FGF23-mediated mechanism.

Mechanistically identical to XLH (FGF23 excess causing renal phosphate wasting) but acquired; must be ruled out via somatostatin receptor imaging despite the long history suggesting a genetic etiology.
Caused by gain-of-function mutations in FGF23 leading to similar biochemical profile (hypophosphatemia, high urine phosphate); can present later in life or have variable penetrance mimicking AS.

The initial clinical diagnosis based on sacroiliac fusion and enthesopathy; however, HLA-B27 negativity and lack of response to biologics/NSAIDs make this less likely as the primary driver compared to metabolic bone disease.

Can cause hyperplastic callus formation and calcification of interosseous membranes that mimic ankylosing spondylitis radiographically, though it typically lacks the specific hypophosphatemic biochemical signature seen here.
Explains the triad of hypophosphatemic rickets (bowing/fractures), dental abscesses, and hearing loss as a single unifying genetic etiology that mimics AS radiographically.
A strong alternative for adult-onset hypophosphatemia with renal phosphate wasting, though less likely to explain childhood onset symptoms like hearing loss and dental issues.
The primary misdiagnosis; fails to account for hypophosphatemia, subtrochanteric fractures, or extra-skeletal features like hearing loss and poor dentition.
Clinically similar to XLH but typically presents later in life without the severe childhood skeletal deformities and early hearing loss seen here.
Explains fractures and hearing loss but does not account for the specific biochemical profile of renal phosphate wasting and hypophosphatemia.

Classic triad of hypophosphatemia with renal phosphate wasting, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and enthesopathy mimicking AS; hearing loss and dental abscesses are hallmark extra-skeletal manifestations.

Acquired form of hypophosphatemic rickets causing similar biochemical profile and bone pain/fractures; must be ruled out via FGF23 levels and somatostatin receptor imaging despite the long history favoring genetic cause.
Initial clinical diagnosis based on sacroiliac fusion and spinal stiffness, but HLA-B27 negativity and atypical femoral bowing/fractures make this a likely misdiagnosis or incidental comorbidity.
Clinically indistinguishable from XLH in adults regarding skeletal and dental findings; requires family history analysis to differentiate from X-linked inheritance.
Can present with adult-onset fractures, hearing loss, and dentinogenesis imperfecta, but typically lacks the specific hypophosphatemia and renal phosphate wasting seen here.
Classic triad of childhood-onset hearing loss, dental abscesses due to dentin defects, and adult osteomalacia with hypophosphatemia and renal phosphate wasting; often misdiagnosed as AS.
Acquired hypophosphatemic rickets mimicking XLH symptoms in adults; requires exclusion via FGF23 levels and imaging for phosphaturic mesenchymal tumors given the late presentation of fractures.
Retained as a differential due to sacroiliac fusion and enthesopathy, but HLA-B27 negativity and atypical femoral bowing make this less likely than metabolic bone disease.
Clinically indistinguishable from XLH regarding phosphate wasting and skeletal deformities; genetic testing required to differentiate based on family history patterns not fully detailed here.
Long-term hydrocodone use may contribute to secondary osteoporosis and fracture risk, though it does not explain the specific biochemical profile of hypophosphatemia and high ALP.
Most common benign salivary gland tumor of the palate; slow growth, firm/rubbery consistency, and normal radiograph fit classic presentation.
Reactive gingival lesion often triggered by trauma/prosthesis; can present as a firm nodule with potential calcifications not always visible on panoramic X-ray early on.
Soft to firm, rubbery, gray-white appearance; well-defined but unencapsulated; can occur in oral cavity without systemic NF1 signs.
Encapsulated, slow-growing, painless mass; histology shows Antoni A/B patterns; less common than PA but fits gross description.
Most common malignant salivary gland tumor; can mimic benign lesions clinically; requires exclusion due to progressive enlargement.
Classic presentation of a slow-growing, painless, firm, lobulated palatal mass with normal overlying mucosa and radiographically silent bone involvement.
Common gingival reactive lesion that can mimic neoplasms; however, the lack of calcification on panoramic radiography makes this less likely than salivary origin.
Can present as a well-circumscribed, encapsulated, rubbery nodule in the oral cavity, though palatal location is less common than tongue or floor of mouth.
The most common malignant salivary gland tumor of the palate; must be ruled out due to progressive enlargement, though typically presents with more aggressive features or ulceration.
Considered given the history of prior surgery at the site, but the large size (3.0 cm) and lack of pain make this diagnosis highly improbable compared to neoplastic processes.
